questions.q: In many star stories, one constellation is pictured as a hunter, with three stars in its middle forming the hunter's belt. Which constellation is it?
questions.a: Orion

questions.q: On a camping trip in Uttarakhand, Kavya's teacher says, 'If you can find the Pole Star, you can find North.' Why is the Pole Star useful for this in the Northern hemisphere?
questions.a: It appears nearly stationary in the North.
o: It appears nearly stationary in the North.
It is the brightest star in the whole night sky.
It twinkles much more than all the other stars.
It rises in the east every evening after sunset.

questions.q:
Match each description in Column I with the constellation in Column II.
Column I: 1. Pictured as a hunter with a three-star belt  2. Pictured as the hunter's dog; contains the brightest star of the night sky  3. Pictured as a bull that the hunter battles  4. Contains the Little Dipper and the Pole Star
Column II: A. Taurus  B. Orion  C. Ursa Minor  D. Canis Major

Read the statements about stars and constellations.
I. An internationally agreed set of constellation boundaries was defined in the early twentieth century.
II. Stars shine by reflecting the light of the Sun, just as the Moon does.
III. Recognising stars and their patterns is still used in emergencies as a backup method of finding direction.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The International Astronomical Union (IAU) defined an internationally agreed set of constellation boundaries.
Reason (R): Different cultures had marked the boundaries of constellations in different ways.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What does the term 'constellation' refer to today, after the International Astronomical Union listed 88 of them? (b) Name one constellation and one star that lies in it.
questions.a: (a) A constellation is now a defined region of the sky; the IAU divided the entire sky into 88 such regions, which often include patterns of stars. (b) Any one correct pair, for example: Canis Major, which contains Sirius; or Ursa Minor, which contains the Pole Star (in the Little Dipper).
s: (a) States that a constellation is now a defined region of the sky (the sky is divided into 88 regions)
(b) Names a constellation with a star in it, such as Canis Major with Sirius or Ursa Minor with the Pole Star

questions.q: True or False: 'Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is one of the stars of the constellation Orion.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, but it lies in the constellation Canis Major (pictured as the hunter's dog), not in Orion. It is only located close to Orion.
s: States False
Corrects it: Sirius lies in Canis Major, close to Orion, not in Orion

questions.q: A star poster of Orion shows red lines joining some stars and green lines marking an area around them. Kunal says, 'Both kinds of lines are only there to help us. Even with a good telescope, we will not see any red or green lines joining or surrounding Orion's stars in the real sky.' Check Kunal's claim. Say what each colour of line shows, and give your verdict with a reason.
questions.a: Kunal is right. The red lines show the pattern of stars (the imaginary hunter shape) and the green lines show the region of the sky that is the constellation. Neither kind of line exists in the sky; they are imaginary lines drawn on charts only for easy identification, so no telescope can show them.
s: Red lines show the pattern formed by the stars
Green lines show the region of the sky defined as the constellation
Verdict: the claim is correct, because the lines are imaginary and drawn only for easy identification

questions.q:
A planetarium sky chart has five numbered labels. Name what each label points to.
(a) Label 1: three bright stars in a short straight line in the middle of a hunter figure.
(b) Label 2: the whole hunter figure itself.
(c) Label 3: a very bright star in the figure of the hunter's dog, the brightest star of the night sky.
(d) Label 4: a large cup-and-handle pattern of stars in the northern sky, lying in the constellation Ursa Major.
(e) Label 5: a star that is not very bright, part of a smaller cup-and-handle pattern, which appears nearly stationary in the North.
questions.a: (a) The belt of Orion (the hunter's belt). (b) The constellation Orion. (c) Sirius. (d) The Big Dipper. (e) The Pole Star (Polaris), part of the Little Dipper.
s: (a) Names the belt of Orion
(b) Names the constellation Orion
(c) Names Sirius
(d) Names the Big Dipper
(e) Names the Pole Star (Polaris)

questions.q:
A small fishing boat is returning to a village on the Konkan coast at night. The village lies to the north of the boat. Its GPS set has stopped working and the crew has no magnetic compass on board. The sky is clear and dark, with hundreds of stars visible. Two stars catch the crew's attention: a very bright, sparkling star in one part of the sky, and a much fainter star that seems to stay almost in one place in the northern sky.
(a) How did recognising stars and their patterns help sailors in the days before modern technology?
(b) Which star should the crew look for to find North, and why that star?
(c) Name the star pattern, and the constellation, that this star belongs to.
(d) A young sailor says, 'Let us steer by the very bright star, since it is the easiest to see.' The oldest crew member wants to steer by the fainter star instead. Whose plan should they follow? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Recognising stars and their patterns helped sailors and travellers find directions at sea or on land, before modern technology or even the magnetic compass; it is still used as a backup in emergencies. (b) The Pole Star, because it appears nearly stationary in the North direction, so it shows North in the Northern hemisphere. (c) It is part of the Little Dipper, which lies in the constellation Ursa Minor. (d) The oldest crew member's plan. The fainter star staying in the north is the Pole Star, which marks North, the direction of their village. Being bright makes a star easy to see, but brightness does not tell you a direction; only a star that stays nearly fixed in one direction can guide them home.
s: (a) Star patterns helped sailors and travellers find directions before modern technology and the compass
(b) The Pole Star, because it appears nearly stationary in the North
(c) The Little Dipper, in the constellation Ursa Minor
(d) Chooses the fainter star (Pole Star): it stays in the north and gives the direction, while brightness alone gives no direction

questions.q: On a summer night, at about 9 p.m., in which part of the sky should you look to find the Big Dipper?
questions.a: The northern part of the sky
o: The northern part of the sky
The southern part of the sky
The western sky, just after sunset
The eastern sky, just before sunrise

questions.q: Tara packs for a night sky watching trip with her uncle: printouts of a few constellations, a notebook and a magnetic compass. What is the compass for?
questions.a: To find directions, such as north
o: To find directions, such as north
To make the faint stars look brighter
To measure how far away each star is
To block the light coming from street lamps

questions.q: Aman watches the sky from the terrace of his building in Kolkata. Bright lamps on the terrace and on the next building are always on, and he sees only a few stars. Which one change would most help him see more stars from the same terrace?
questions.a: Getting the nearby bright lamps switched off
o: Getting the nearby bright lamps switched off
Watching on a night when the full Moon is up
Shining a strong torch up at the sky
Looking up as soon as he walks out of a lit room

questions.q:
Assertion (A): From the middle of a big city, only a few stars are seen even on a cloudless night.
Reason (R): Stars stop shining when there is a lot of artificial light near them.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about watching the night sky.
I. Not all stars and constellations are visible from all places on Earth on all nights of the year.
II. Because the Pole Star is not very bright, a night with neither the Moon nor clouds is best for spotting it.
III. In India, Orion is best viewed from December to April after sunset.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III

questions.q: True or False: 'Even on a clear, dark night, a person whose house is surrounded by tall buildings and trees may see fewer stars than a person standing in an open field.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Tall buildings and trees can block the view of the sky, so fewer stars can be seen. The night sky is best viewed from open, dark areas.
s: States True
Reason: tall buildings and trees block the view; open dark areas are best for viewing

questions.q: (a) What is light pollution? (b) Apart from light pollution, state one other reason why only a few stars are seen in a big city.
questions.a: (a) Light pollution is the presence of excessive artificial light at night time. (b) Any one: smoke and dust in the city air; or tall buildings and trees that block the view of the sky.
s: (a) Excessive artificial light at night time
(b) One other reason: smoke and dust, or tall buildings and trees blocking the view

questions.q: Ishaan plans his first night sky watching. On a full-Moon night, he will go alone to the brightly lit terrace of his building at 9 p.m. and start searching for the Pole Star the moment he steps out of his lit room. Point out three mistakes in his plan and say what he should do instead for each.
questions.a: Any three: (1) He is going alone; he should go only with an adult. (2) The terrace is brightly lit; he should choose a dark, open place away from lights, tall buildings and trees. (3) He chose a full-Moon night; for the Pole Star, which is not very bright, he should choose a night when neither the Moon nor clouds are visible. (4) He starts at once; he should wait about half an hour for his eyes to adjust to the darkness.
s: First mistake named with the correct fix (e.g. going alone: go with an adult)
Second mistake named with the correct fix (e.g. lit terrace: choose a dark open place away from lights)
Third mistake named with the correct fix (e.g. full Moon: choose a night with no Moon or clouds; or wait about half an hour for the eyes to adjust)

questions.q: On a printed sky chart, the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup are 1.8 cm apart. Mira draws a straight line through them, away from the cup, and finds three stars on the line: star X at 4 cm, star Y at 9 cm and star Z at 15 cm from the nearer cup star. (a) Which star should be the Pole Star? Show your working. (b) Towards which direction does this line point in the real sky? (c) Why would Mira find the real Pole Star hard to spot on a full-Moon night?
questions.a: (a) Star Y. The Pole Star lies at about five times the distance between the two cup stars: 5 x 1.8 cm = 9 cm. (b) Towards the north. (c) The Pole Star is not very bright, so the moonlight makes it hard to see; a night without the Moon or clouds is better.
s: (a) 5 x 1.8 = 9 cm, so star Y
(b) The line points towards the north
(c) The Pole Star is not very bright, so moonlight makes it hard to see

questions.q: Anu lives in Bhopal, in the Northern hemisphere. Her pen-friend Zoe lives in Cape Town, in the southern hemisphere. Both want to find North at night using the stars. (a) Can Anu use the Pole Star to find North? Give a reason. (b) Can Zoe use the Pole Star in the same way? Give a reason. (c) Zoe's brother says, 'Just use a bigger telescope and you will find the Pole Star from Cape Town.' Is he right? (d) How can Zoe find out which stars and constellations she can see from her location, and when?
questions.a: (a) Yes. The Pole Star appears nearly stationary in the North direction, which helps to locate North in the Northern hemisphere. (b) No. The Pole Star is not visible from the southern hemisphere of Earth, so Zoe cannot use it. (c) No. The problem is not that the Pole Star is too faint for her eyes; it is not visible from the southern hemisphere at all, so a bigger telescope does not help. (d) She can use a sky mapping app on a mobile phone, or other online resources, to find when and in which part of the sky a star or constellation will be visible from her location.
s: (a) Yes: the Pole Star appears nearly stationary in the North, useful in the Northern hemisphere
(b) No: the Pole Star is not visible from the southern hemisphere
(c) No: it is not visible from there at all, so a bigger telescope does not help
(d) Uses a sky mapping app or online resources to find what is visible from her location and when

questions.q:
The Class 6 eco-club of a school near Jaipur is holding a sky watching evening on 15 January, starting at 8 p.m., in a dark playground away from lights. The teacher wants every student to find the constellation Orion first and then a very bright star near it. One student has never seen Orion before. The club is also thinking of a second evening in July.
(a) Which stars should the new student look for first to find Orion, and why?
(b) Once Orion is found, along which line and in which direction should the students look to find the very bright star near it?
(c) Name that very bright star.
(d) Should the club plan to show Orion again at the July evening? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The three bright stars in a short straight line around the middle of Orion (the hunter's belt); finding them first is the easiest way to find Orion. (b) Along an imaginary straight line through the three middle stars of Orion, looking towards the east. (c) Sirius. (d) No. In India, Orion is best viewed from December to April after sunset; July is outside this period, so the club should show Orion on a December to April evening such as 15 January.
s: (a) The three stars in a short line in the middle (the belt): the easiest way to find Orion
(b) Along a line through the three belt stars, towards the east
(c) Names Sirius
(d) No: Orion is best viewed in India from December to April after sunset, and July is outside this

questions.q: Going outwards from the Sun, which planet comes immediately after the Earth?
questions.a: Mars

questions.q: Using the order of the eight planets from the Sun, how many planets lie between the Earth and Saturn?
Arya wants to spot Venus at dawn from her balcony in Chennai. Where and when should she look?
questions.a: Near the eastern direction, before sunrise
o: Near the eastern direction, before sunrise
Near the western direction, before sunrise
Near the northern direction, at midnight
Near the southern direction, at noon

questions.q:
Read the statements about the planets.
I. Mars appears red because it is the hottest planet.
II. The four giant planets have large flat ring-like structures made of dust particles and rocky material.
III. In general, the farther a planet is from the Sun, the colder it is.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Venus is a star, and that is why it is called the Morning Star or the Evening Star.
Reason (R): Venus is usually seen shining brightly at dawn and at dusk.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: (a) Differentiate between the rotation and the revolution of the Earth. (b) About how long does the Earth take for one rotation, and for one revolution?
questions.a: (a) Rotation is the Earth spinning about its own axis; revolution is the Earth moving around the Sun. (b) One rotation takes about 24 hours (a day); one revolution takes nearly one year.
s: (a) Rotation: spinning about its axis; revolution: moving around the Sun
(b) About 24 hours for a rotation and nearly one year for a revolution

questions.q: True or False: 'Pluto, which lies farther than Neptune and revolves around the Sun, is the ninth planet of our Solar System.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Pluto was called a planet when it was discovered, but in 2006 the International Astronomical Union redefined what a planet is; Pluto is now called a dwarf planet. Our Solar System has eight planets, ending with Neptune.
s: States False
Corrects it: since the IAU's 2006 definition Pluto is a dwarf planet; there are eight planets

questions.q: Take 1 astronomical unit (au) as 150 million km, about the distance between the Sun and the Earth. Space probe A is 4 au from the Sun. Space probe B is 300 million km from the Sun. (a) How far is probe A from the Sun in million km? (b) Which probe is farther from the Sun, and by how many au?
questions.a: (a) 4 x 150 = 600 million km. (b) Probe B is 300 / 150 = 2 au from the Sun, so probe A is farther, by 4 - 2 = 2 au.
s: (a) 4 x 150 = 600 million km
(b) B is 2 au away, so A is farther by 2 au

questions.q: Give the reason for each name. (a) Mars is called the Red Planet. (b) The Earth is called the Blue Planet. (c) Venus is called the Morning Star or the Evening Star, even though it is not a star.
questions.a: (a) Mars appears red because the soil on Mars is reddish in colour. (b) A large portion of the Earth's surface is covered with water, so it appears blue from space. (c) Venus is usually seen shining brightly at dawn and at dusk.
s: (a) The soil on Mars is reddish
(b) Much of the Earth's surface is covered with water, so it looks blue from space
(c) Venus is seen shining brightly at dawn and dusk

questions.q:
On a clear evening in Shimla, about 40 minutes after sunset, Ritika and her father notice three objects in the sky. Object 1 is very bright, low in the western sky, and shines steadily. Object 2 is a reddish dot that also shines steadily. Object 3, high in the sky, is a point of light that twinkles a lot. Their sky app is not working, so they must reason it out.
(a) Is Object 3 more likely a star or a planet? Give a reason.
(b) Which planet is Object 1 most likely to be? Give one clue from the observation.
(c) Which planet is Object 2 most likely to be, and why does that planet look reddish?
(d) Ritika's father says, 'Object 1 cannot be a planet, because planets are too far away to be seen without a telescope.' Is he right? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A star, because stars appear to twinkle a lot, unlike planets. (b) Venus: it is very bright (the brightest object in the sky after the Sun and the Moon) and is seen near the western direction after sunset. (c) Mars, the Red Planet; it appears red because the soil on Mars is reddish in colour. (d) No. Venus, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can all be seen with the naked eye; they are so far away that they look like shining dots, just like stars. A telescope is needed only for dim objects that the naked eye cannot see.
s: (a) A star, because stars twinkle a lot and planets generally do not
(b) Venus, with a clue: very bright, or seen in the west after sunset
(c) Mars, which looks red because its soil is reddish
(d) He is wrong: Venus, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can be seen with the naked eye as shining dots

questions.q:
Class 6 students want to build a model of the Sun and the Earth. They use a bead 2 cm across for the Earth. Use these facts: the Sun is about 100 times bigger than the Earth in diameter; the Sun is about 150 million km from the Earth; take the Earth's diameter as about 12,800 km.
(a) How wide should the model Sun be, in cm and in m?
(b) The real Sun-Earth distance is how many Earth-diameters? How far from the model Sun should the bead be placed, to the nearest metre?
(c) The real Sun is so much bigger than the Earth. Why does it look small in our sky?
(d) Why does a picture of the Solar System in a book usually say 'not to scale'?
(e) The students have a 10 m long corridor. Can they keep the 2 cm bead and still place the Sun and the Earth at the correct scale distance? If not, about how big would the Earth bead and the Sun ball have to be for the distance to fit in exactly 10 m? Judge which choice they should make.
questions.a: (a) 100 x 2 cm = 200 cm = 2 m. (b) 150,000,000 / 12,800 = 11,718.75, about 11,719 Earth-diameters; 11,718.75 x 2 cm = 23,437.5 cm, about 234 m. (c) Because it is very far from the Earth (about 150 million km). (d) To fit the figure within a page, the sizes and distances of the objects cannot be drawn in their actual proportions. (e) No: 234 m does not fit in a 10 m corridor. Shrinking the whole model by 10 / 234.375 makes the Earth bead about 2 x 10 / 234.375 = 0.085 cm (under 1 mm) and the Sun ball about 8.5 cm. The judgement: either use these tiny sizes to show the true distance, or keep the 2 cm bead and 2 m Sun to show true sizes and say that the distance is not to scale; one model cannot show both at this size in the corridor.
s: (b) About 11,719 Earth-diameters, so about 234 m
(c) It looks small because it is very far away
(d) Sizes and distances cannot fit a page in true proportion, so figures are not to scale
(e) No; for 10 m the bead is about 0.085 cm and the Sun about 8.5 cm; judges that one model shows either true sizes or true distance, not both

questions.q: The Moon takes about 27 days to complete one revolution around the Earth. About how many revolutions does it complete in 81 days?
Photographs of the Moon taken by ISRO show many circular, bowl-like structures on its surface. What are these structures called?
questions.a: Craters

questions.q:
Match each of India's Moon missions in Column I with the correct detail in Column II.
Column I: 1. Chandrayaan-1  2. Chandrayaan-2  3. Chandrayaan-3  4. Chandrayaan-4
Column II: A. Launched in 2019  B. Being planned, to bring back soil and rock samples from the Moon  C. India's first mission to the Moon, launched in 2008  D. Its lander soft-landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023

Assertion (A): The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth.
Reason (R): The Moon is about a quarter the size of the Earth in diameter.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about satellites and the Moon.
I. Satellites are larger in size than the planets they move around.
II. There is hardly any atmosphere on the Moon.
III. Mars has more moons than Jupiter.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II only

questions.q: (a) Name the lander of Chandrayaan-3 and the rover it carried. (b) Why does India celebrate 23 August as 'National Space Day'?
questions.a: (a) The Vikram lander, carrying the Pragyan rover. (b) On 23 August 2023, the Vikram lander soft-landed near the Moon's south pole, making India the first country in the world to land near the little explored south pole; 23 August was declared National Space Day to mark this success.
s: (a) Vikram (lander) and Pragyan (rover)
(b) Marks the 23 August 2023 soft landing near the Moon's south pole, the first by any country

questions.q: The Moon takes about 27 days to complete one revolution around the Earth. In a year of 365 days, (a) how many complete revolutions does it make? (b) how many days are left over after these complete revolutions?
questions.a: (a) 365 / 27 = 13.5 (about), so 13 complete revolutions. (b) 13 x 27 = 351 days, so 365 - 351 = 14 days are left over.
s: (a) 365 / 27 is about 13.5, so 13 complete revolutions
(b) 13 x 27 = 351; 365 - 351 = 14 days left over

questions.q: For a science fair, Farhan makes the Earth as a clay ball 20 cm across. Now he wants to make the Moon. (a) How wide should the Moon ball be? (b) Should he wrap the Moon ball in a thin layer of cotton to show a layer of air, as he did for the Earth? Why? (c) Should he press small bowl-shaped dents into the Moon ball? What made most of these features on the real Moon?
questions.a: (a) The Moon is about a quarter the size of the Earth in diameter: 20 / 4 = 5 cm. (b) No. There is hardly any atmosphere on the Moon. (c) Yes. They show craters, most of which were formed by asteroids or rocks from space hitting the Moon's surface.
s: (a) A quarter of 20 cm: 5 cm
(b) No, because the Moon has hardly any atmosphere
(c) Yes: craters, formed mostly by asteroids or rocks from space hitting the surface

questions.q: A sky-watching club sorts objects by what they move around and what they look like. For each object, say whether it is a planet, a natural satellite (moon) or neither, and give the reason. (a) A large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun. (b) A small object that moves around the planet Mars. (c) A small, rocky, irregularly shaped object that revolves around the Sun between the paths of Mars and Jupiter. (d) An object made of dust, gases, rocks and ice that grows a long tail as it comes close to the Sun.
questions.a: (a) A planet: a planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun. (b) A natural satellite (one of the two moons of Mars), because it moves around a planet. (c) Neither: it is an asteroid; it moves around the Sun, not around a planet, and it is small and irregular, not a large nearly spherical planet. (d) Neither: it is a comet, a visitor from the outer regions of the Solar System that moves around the Sun, not around a planet.
s: (a) Planet: large, nearly spherical, revolves around the Sun
(b) Natural satellite: it moves around a planet (Mars)
(c) Neither (an asteroid): small, irregular, moves around the Sun
(d) Neither (a comet): moves around the Sun and grows a tail near it

questions.q:
A school in Pune is setting up a 'Moon Corner' for National Space Day. The board has a timeline with three years marked on it: 2008, 2019 and 2023. Beside it is a large ISRO photograph of the Moon's surface showing hundreds of round, bowl-like marks, many of them formed very long ago. Two draft banners have been made. Banner P says: 'India: the first country to land on the Moon'. Banner Q says: 'India: the first country to land near the Moon's south pole'.
(a) Write the name of the mission that belongs to each year on the timeline.
(b) How many years passed between India's first Moon mission and its soft landing on the Moon?
(c) A visitor asks why the bowl-like marks, though formed long ago, are still so clear. What should the students say?
(d) Which banner should the school put up? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) 2008: Chandrayaan-1; 2019: Chandrayaan-2; 2023: Chandrayaan-3. (b) 2023 - 2008 = 15 years. (c) They are craters. Since there is no atmosphere, water or life on the Moon, these features stay on the surface for a very long time. (d) Banner Q. With Chandrayaan-3, India became the first country in the world to achieve a landing near the little explored south pole of the Moon. The chapter does not say India was the first country to land on the Moon at all, so Banner P claims more than the facts support.
s: (a) 2008 Chandrayaan-1, 2019 Chandrayaan-2, 2023 Chandrayaan-3
(c) No atmosphere, water or life on the Moon, so craters stay for a very long time
(d) Banner Q: India was the first to land near the Moon's south pole; Banner P claims more than the facts

questions.q: The Sun and the planets are nearly spherical. What is the shape of most asteroids?
questions.a: Irregular

questions.q: Asteroids range in size from about 10 m to about 500 km. Which of these could be the size of an asteroid?
questions.a: 250 km

questions.q: Halley's Comet appears every 76 years, and its last appearance was in 1986. In which of these earlier years should it also have appeared?

Assertion (A): A comet shows its long tail only when it comes close to the Sun.
Reason (R): As a comet approaches the Sun, its frozen material starts evaporating, and this evaporating material forms the tail.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Scientists are tracking a small object that revolves around the Sun. Which observation would show that it is NOT an asteroid?
questions.a: It grows a long tail as it comes close to the Sun.
o: It grows a long tail as it comes close to the Sun.
It is made of rock and is irregular in shape.
Its path lies between those of Mars and Jupiter.
It has passed very close to the Earth more than once.

questions.q: True or False: 'Every comet that comes close to the Sun keeps returning to it again and again.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Many comets do revolve around the Sun and come close to it periodically, but a few comets escape and move out of the Solar System, and a few others break up or fall into the Sun or other planets when they approach them.
s: States False
Corrects it: many return periodically, but a few escape the Solar System and a few break up or fall into the Sun or a planet

questions.q: (a) What is the asteroid belt? (b) Why do scientists keep watch on some asteroids even though most of them stay far away in the belt?
questions.a: (a) The asteroid belt is the region between the paths of Mars and Jupiter in which many asteroids revolve around the Sun. (b) Occasionally, some asteroids pass very close to the Earth.
s: (a) The region between the paths of Mars and Jupiter where many asteroids revolve around the Sun
(b) Some asteroids occasionally pass very close to the Earth

questions.q: Asteroids range in size from about 10 m to about 500 km. (a) Write 500 km in metres. (b) About how many times wider is the largest asteroid than the smallest? (c) A rock 3 m across is found drifting in space near the asteroid belt. Using this size range, can it be called an asteroid? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 500 km = 500 x 1000 m = 5,00,000 m. (b) 5,00,000 / 10 = 50,000 times. (c) No. At 3 m it is smaller than the smallest asteroid size of about 10 m given in the range.
s: (c) No: 3 m is below the smallest size of about 10 m

questions.q:
Astronomers in Kodaikanal tracked a bright object that came in from the outer regions of the Solar System. As it moved closer to the Sun, a long glowing tail appeared. Months later, as it moved away from the Sun, it became dim and could no longer be seen with the naked eye. Its path brings it back close to the Sun every 12 years, and it was last close to the Sun in 2024.
(a) Name this kind of object.
(b) Name any two materials that such an object is made of.
(c) Why did the tail appear as it came closer to the Sun?
(d) Why could it not be seen with the naked eye after it moved away?
(e) In which year should it next come close to the Sun?
questions.a: (a) A comet. (b) Any two of: dust, gases, rocks and ice. (c) As it came close to the Sun, its frozen material started evaporating, and this evaporating material formed the tail. (d) Comets appear dim as they move away from the Sun, so it can no longer be seen with the naked eye. (e) 2024 + 12 = 2036.
s: (a) A comet
(b) Any two of dust, gases, rocks, ice
(c) Frozen material evaporates near the Sun and forms the tail
(d) Comets appear dim as they move away from the Sun

questions.q:
A planetarium in Bhubaneswar is tracking two objects. Object P is about 140 km across, made of rock, irregular in shape, and revolves around the Sun along a path between those of Mars and Jupiter. Object Q is about 8 km across, made of dust, gases, rocks and ice; it is now moving towards the Sun and a faint tail has just started to show. Q will pass closest to the Sun in about 3 months and will be far beyond it in about 8 months. The planetarium can hold only one public telescope night for Q: now, in 3 months, or in 8 months.
(a) What kind of object is P? Give one reason.
(b) What kind of object is Q? Give one reason.
(c) Predict how Q's tail and brightness will change over the next 8 months.
(d) Which date should the planetarium choose for its telescope night for Q? Justify, mentioning any risk.
questions.a: (a) An asteroid: it is small, rocky and irregular in shape, and its path lies in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. (b) A comet: it is made of dust, gases, rocks and ice and is developing a tail as it approaches the Sun. (c) As Q gets closer to the Sun over the next 3 months, more of its frozen material evaporates, so its tail grows and it becomes easier to see; after it passes the Sun and moves away, it appears dim and by 8 months it may not be visible to the naked eye. (d) In about 3 months, when Q is closest to the Sun, because the tail formed by evaporating material should be at its best then; 8 months is the worst choice because comets appear dim as they move away from the Sun. The risk is that a few comets break up or fall into the Sun when they approach it, so a short viewing now, while the tail is faint, can be kept as a backup.
s: (a) Asteroid: small, rocky, irregular, in the belt between Mars and Jupiter
(b) Comet: made of dust, gases, rocks and ice, and growing a tail near the Sun
(c) Tail grows and Q brightens as it nears the Sun; it becomes dim as it moves away
(d) Chooses about 3 months (closest to the Sun) over 8 months, and notes the risk that a comet may break up near the Sun

questions.q: On a moonless night, far from city lights, how does our home galaxy, the Milky Way, appear in the sky?
questions.a: As a faint band of light from near north to south
o: As a faint band of light from near north to south
As a single very bright star that does not twinkle
As a small cup-and-handle pattern of stars in the north
As a bright glowing tail that points away from the Sun

questions.q: From her terrace in Indore, Mansi sees four bright objects: the Moon, Venus, Jupiter and Sirius. Her brother says all four must make their own light because they all look bright. Which one of them actually produces its own light?
questions.a: Sirius

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Galaxy  2. Exoplanet  3. Solar System  4. Universe
Column II: A. A planet discovered revolving around a star other than the Sun  B. The Sun, eight planets, their moons, asteroids and comets  C. A system of millions to billions of stars  D. Contains many galaxies, including the Milky Way

Read the statements.
I. The Sun is the largest and the heaviest object in the Solar System.
II. A galaxy has millions to billions of planets, but only a few stars.
III. Exoplanets are the planets that revolve around the Sun beyond Neptune.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Milky Way Galaxy is called our home galaxy.
Reason (R): A galaxy has millions to billions of stars.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is a galaxy? (b) Name the galaxy that our Solar System is part of.
questions.a: (a) A galaxy is a huge system that has millions to billions of stars. (b) The Milky Way Galaxy (our home galaxy).
s: (a) A galaxy has millions to billions of stars
(b) The Milky Way Galaxy

questions.q: True or False: 'Our whole Solar System is only a small part of the Milky Way Galaxy.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The Milky Way Galaxy has millions to billions of stars, and our Sun is just one star; the Sun with its planets, moons, asteroids and comets makes up the Solar System, which is a part of the Milky Way.
s: States True
Reason: the Milky Way has millions to billions of stars and the Solar System, around one star (the Sun), is part of it

questions.q: Write these four in order, from the smallest to the largest: the Milky Way Galaxy, the Earth, the Universe, the Solar System. Then answer: (a) Which objects, besides the Sun, make up the Solar System? (b) What lies beyond the Milky Way Galaxy?
questions.a: Order: the Earth, the Solar System, the Milky Way Galaxy, the Universe. (a) The eight planets, their moons, and many smaller objects including asteroids and comets. (b) Many other galaxies, in outer space; together they are part of the Universe.
s: Correct order: Earth, Solar System, Milky Way Galaxy, Universe
(a) Eight planets, their moons, asteroids and comets
(b) Many other galaxies

questions.q: Looking at the faint band of the Milky Way from a village in Ladakh, Priya says, 'That band is a galaxy with a huge number of stars, but our Sun is not one of them, because the Sun is not in that band.' Check each part of her claim and give your verdict.
questions.a: Priya is partly right. The band is the Milky Way Galaxy, and a galaxy does have millions to billions of stars, so the first part is correct. But our Solar System, with the Sun, is part of the Milky Way Galaxy; it is our home galaxy, so the Sun is one of its stars even though we see the band elsewhere in the sky. The second part is wrong.
s: Agrees the band is a galaxy with millions to billions of stars
Shows the second part is wrong: the Solar System, with the Sun, is part of the Milky Way (our home galaxy)
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
A school photography club wants to photograph the Milky Way on the same date and time, from one of four places. Place A: the rooftop of a building in the centre of Delhi, clear sky, no Moon. Place B: an open field near a village 90 km from the city, clear sky, full Moon. Place C: the same open field, clear sky, no Moon. Place D: the same open field, no Moon, but thick clouds.
(a) If they succeed, what will they see in the sky?
(b) Why should they reject Place A?
(c) Why should they reject Place B?
(d) Why should they reject Place D?
(e) Which place should they choose? Give two things they should do after reaching it, so that they can see the Milky Way well and stay safe.
questions.a: (a) An extended faint band of light stretching from near north to south across the sky: the Milky Way Galaxy. (b) A city centre has light pollution, smoke and dust, so faint objects are hard to see; the Milky Way is seen from dark locations away from city lights. (c) The Milky Way is seen in a moonless sky; the bright full Moon will wash out the faint band. (d) Thick clouds block the view of the sky. (e) Place C, the dark, open, cloudless field with no Moon. Any two: go only with adults; wait about half an hour after reaching for their eyes to adjust to the darkness; keep away from lights, tall buildings and trees.
s: (a) A faint band of light from near north to south (the Milky Way)
(b) Rejects A: city lights (light pollution), smoke and dust
(c) Rejects B: the Milky Way needs a moonless sky
(d) Rejects D: clouds block the view
(e) Chooses C with two steps such as going with adults and waiting about half an hour for the eyes to adjust
